title: An instruction length decoder
description:
Write the length decoder at the heart of every disassembler and hooking library (lesson 5.01), for a common subset of x64:

```cpp
std::size_t instructionLength(const std::vector<std::uint8_t>& code, std::size_t at);
```

It returns the length of the instruction starting at `code[at]`, or **0** if the bytes are not in the subset or run out before the instruction ends.

1. **Prefixes**: any number of `66`, `F2`, `F3`, then optionally one REX byte (`40`-`4F`).
2. **Opcode** and what follows it:

| Opcode | Then |
|---|---|
| `50`-`5F`, `90`, `C3`, `CC` | nothing |
| `70`-`7F`, `EB` | 1-byte displacement |
| `E8`, `E9` | 4-byte displacement |
| `B8`-`BF` | 4-byte immediate, or 8 with REX.W |
| `01 03 29 2B 31 33 39 3B 63 85 89 8B 8D` | ModRM |
| `83` | ModRM, then 1-byte immediate |
| `81`, `C7` | ModRM, then 4-byte immediate (2 bytes with a `66` prefix) |
| `0F 80`-`0F 8F` | 4-byte displacement |
| `0F 1F`, `0F B6`, `0F B7`, `0F BE`, `0F BF` | ModRM |

3. **ModRM** (lesson 5.01's table): `mod` 11 adds nothing; otherwise `rm` 100 adds a SIB byte (and 4 more bytes if the SIB base is 101 with `mod` 00); `mod` 00 with `rm` 101 adds 4; `mod` 01 adds 1; `mod` 10 adds 4.
hints: Work through the instruction in order with a moving index: skip prefixes, note REX.W and the `66` prefix, read the opcode, then add the sizes of what that opcode needs. Do the ModRM part in its own function that returns "ModRM byte + SIB + displacement".
The special cases live entirely in the ModRM rules: `rm` 100 means a SIB byte follows, and a SIB base of 101 with `mod` 00 means a 4-byte displacement instead of a base register.
